planting.note: Sow in shallow furrows about 2cm deep after a thorough pre-irrigation; avoid sowing during the hottest part of summer, as high soil temperatures reduce germination.

directions: This clump-forming wild onion from the Mongolian and Central Asian steppe produces thin hollow leaves and dense umbels of violet-red flowers, and is prized for extreme drought and cold tolerance on poor sandy soils. Grow it in full sun with excellent drainage and low humidity; it tolerates repeated close cutting like a chive once established. Clumps can be divided for propagation, but seed-grown plantings establish well if kept moist until emergence, which can take two to three weeks.

common_name: MI-2 Chili Pepper (Sri Lankan Dry-Zone Open-Pollinated Chile)

planting.note: Start indoors and transplant after soil has warmed well past the last frost, since this variety was bred for a tropical dry-zone climate with no cold tolerance.

directions: MI-2 is a tall, erect open-pollinated chili released by Sri Lanka's Department of Agriculture at Maha Illuppallama in 1973 as a selection from the earlier MI-1 line, and it remains one of the most widely grown chili varieties in Sri Lanka. Plants bear medium-sized, slightly curved, deep red pods with moderate heat and an earthy, balanced flavor well suited to drying, powdering, and chili flakes. It performs well in rainfed upland and dry-zone conditions and shows useful tolerance of leaf curl complex. Expect green chili yields in the range of 12 to 15 tonnes per hectare under good management.
sources: Department of Agriculture, Sri Lanka — HORDI chili variety records
HARTI (Hector Kobbekaduwa Agrarian Research and Training Institute), 'Local Hybrid Chili Cultivation and Dry Chili Production'

common_name: MC 43 Bitter Gourd (Sri Lankan Island-Wide Heirloom Selection)

planting.note: Direct sow in warm soil once frost danger has passed and provide a trellis, since this is a climbing vine that fruits best when trained off the ground.

directions: MC 43 is a long-established local selection released in 1940 and recommended for island-wide cultivation by Sri Lanka's Department of Agriculture, producing medium-sized, light greenish-white fruit with a dentate skin surface and only light bitterness compared with darker-skinned types. It is a vigorous climbing vine best grown on an overhead trellis for straight, clean fruit. Typical trellised yields run 15 to 20 tonnes per hectare.
sources: Department of Agriculture, Sri Lanka — HORDI bitter gourd variety records (doa.gov.lk)

common_name: Thinnaweli Purple Brinjal (Sri Lankan Wet-Zone Heirloom Eggplant)

planting.note: Transplant into warm soil after frost risk has passed; this heirloom was selected for the wet and intermediate zones of Sri Lanka rather than for cool-season tolerance.

directions: Thinnaweli Purple is one of the brinjal varieties recommended by Sri Lanka's Department of Agriculture for the island's wet and intermediate zones, producing cylindrical fruit marked with light purple lines over a white background. The plant carries light purple flowers on a green stem with green leaf ribs, and the variety is valued chiefly for its resistance to bacterial wilt, a common limiting disease in brinjal production. It reaches first harvest in about 75 to 80 days from transplanting and performs best with consistent moisture and fertile, well-drained soil.
sources: Department of Agriculture, Sri Lanka — HORDI brinjal variety records (doa.gov.lk)

common_name: MI 5 Okra (Sri Lankan Island-Wide Open-Pollinated Okra)

planting.note: Direct sow after soil has warmed well above 70F, as okra seed germinates slowly and poorly in cold ground.

directions: MI 5 was released in 1975 by Sri Lanka's Department of Agriculture and remains a staple open-pollinated okra grown throughout the wet and intermediate zones year-round, with cultivation in the dry zone mainly limited to the Maha season. Pods are light green, medium-sized, and pyramidal with seven to nine distinct edges, and stems show light anthocyanin pigmentation. First harvest typically comes at 55 to 60 days, though the variety is susceptible to mosaic virus in humid conditions.
sources: Department of Agriculture, Sri Lanka — HORDI okra variety records (doa.gov.lk)

common_name: TA-2 Snake Gourd (Sri Lankan Long-Fruited Heirloom Selection)

planting.note: Direct sow in warm, well-drained, organically rich soil once frost danger is past, and provide an overhead trellis so the long fruit can hang straight.

directions: TA-2 is a long-fruited snake gourd variety released by Sri Lanka's Department of Agriculture, producing fruit longer than a meter with a whitish-ash surface that develops faint green stripes as it matures. It is a heavy-yielding, aggressively climbing vine well suited to dry and intermediate zone cultivation during the Maha season, with potential yields of 25 to 30 tonnes per hectare under favorable irrigation. First harvest comes quickly, at about 45 to 55 days from sowing.
sources: Department of Agriculture, Sri Lanka — HORDI snake gourd variety records (doa.gov.lk)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in deep, moist, humus-rich soil in a sheltered, partly shaded site, keeping young plants shielded from drying wind.

directions: One of the tallest canopy trees of the Macaronesian laurisilva, til carries glossy, leathery leaves and small yellow-green flowers typical of the laurel family, with the common name referring to the unpleasant smell released when its wood is freshly cut. It is native to the cloud-forest zones of Madeira, the Canary Islands, and the Azores, where it grows in the cool, constantly humid shade of the forest interior. In cultivation it demands the same sheltered, evenly moist, frost-free conditions, performing best in a woodland garden setting on the mildest coasts with protection from strong sun and wind while establishing.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens Kew — Plants of the World Online
